title: Kenya's Soil Doctors: Reading the Ground Before Planting
title_zh: 肯尼亚的“土壤医生”：播种之前先读懂土地
source_name: UN News — “Soil mapping aims to boost agricultural production in Kenya” (23 Oct 2026)
summary_zh: 肯尼亚正在推进“土壤测绘促进农业粮食系统韧性”（SoilFER）项目，由联合国粮农组织（FAO）和肯尼亚农业与畜牧研究组织（KALRO）合作实施，美国国务院和日本提供资金。项目已在 45 个县采集并测绘了 3,600 多份土壤样本，绘制数字土壤地图，检测结果直接发送到农民手机上，帮助他们决定该用哪种肥料、用多少。部分农民接受培训成为“土壤医生”，再教给其他农民。受访农民说，过去大家常常过量施用化肥，“现在我们懂了”。肯尼亚农业部长呼吁：种什么、施什么肥之前，先做土壤检测。该项目还在加纳、危地马拉等另外六个国家实施。
paragraphs: For many small farmers, deciding how to grow food has always involved a lot of guesswork. Which fertilizer should they buy? How much should they use? In Kenya, a new programme is trying to replace that guesswork with reliable data, and it starts with something most people never think about: the soil under their feet.

The programme is called SoilFER, which stands for Soil Mapping for Resilient Agrifood Systems. It is run by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) together with the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO), with financial support from the United States and Japan. So far, more than 3,600 soil samples have been collected across 45 counties. The results are being used to build a digital soil map that gives farmers information about their own land, and the findings are sent directly to their mobile phones.

Why does this matter? Climate shocks such as drought and heavy rain are becoming more frequent, and farmers cannot afford to waste money or damage their land. Without proper information, many have simply added more chemicals in the hope of higher yields. "Now we know better," said Agness Munialo, a farmer from western Kenya. She is one of a group of farmers who have been trained as "soil doctors". They learn to diagnose problems such as poor fertility or the wrong pH level, and then they pass this knowledge on to their neighbours.

The project is also changing how some young people see farming. A young intern at KALRO said that once she understood soil testing, she became more interested in working on her family's farm. Meanwhile, three laboratories have been renovated and equipped with modern technology to analyse the samples.

Kenya's agriculture minister, Mutahi Kagwe, encouraged all Kenyans to think about soil testing before they decide what to plant or which fertilizer to use. He also called for closer cooperation between agricultural institutions so that data is shared rather than kept separately. SoilFER is now running in six other countries as well, including Ghana, Guatemala and Zambia. Its message is simple: if we want healthy crops and secure food supplies, we first need to understand the ground they grow in.
